title: A hymn in Dhanasri
hookLine: Dhanasri holds Guru Nanak's sky aarti, and near its end, the Bhagats' aartis

cards: Aarti is a way of honoring what is dear by waving light before it: a tray of small flames, lifted and circled slowly.
Back in year two, you met Guru Nanak's hymn that takes the tray and throws it wide: the sky is the platter, the sun and moon are its lamps, the stars are pearls. It lives in Raga Dhanasri.
Keep turning the pages of Dhanasri to the end, and more aartis are waiting, sung by the Bhagats. Today: a hymn in Dhanasri, and the conversation its aartis have.

teach.b: Start with Guru Nanak's hymn, gagan mai thaal, the sky as the platter. The wind is incense, the forests are flowers, and the whole universe is already performing the aarti. Nobody needs to light anything.
Now the end of the raga, where the Bhagats' hymns sit.

teach.h: RAVIDAS: YOUR NAME IS MY AARTI.
teach.b: Ravidas, remembered by tradition as a leather worker, sings in paraphrase: your Name is my aarti and my cleansing bath.
Then he takes the tray apart: your Name is the lamp, the oil, the wick; without the Name, everything else is show.
Sain, remembered as a barber, prepares incense, lamp and ghee for an aarti, and says he would give himself for the Lord.
Dhanna, remembered as a farmer, opens with the word aarta, which some readers hear as an aarti and others as the cry of a humble petitioner.

He asks plainly for what a household needs: lentils and flour and ghee, shoes and clothes, a milk cow, a good horse, a good wife. Guru Nanak lifts the aarti to the sky. Ravidas brings it inward, into the Name.
Sain holds the lamp with devotion. Dhanna sets it on the kitchen table.

teach.h: ONE RAGA, MANY KINDS OF HEART.
teach.b: The Granth keeps all four voices in one raga.
And the whole week ran the same way: longing at night in Bihagra, wedding and mourning in Vadhans, steady faith and calm in Sorath, true wealth in Dhanasri. One raga, many kinds of heart.

how: Guru Nanak's gagan mai thaal is part of the Kirtan Sohila said at night and is sung in kirtan; the Bhagats' aarti hymns from the end of Dhanasri are also sung, and some Sikh congregations sing a sequence of these aartis together.

games.q: what does “a hymn in dhanasri” mean?
o: a lament that opens by blessing the Creator
Nanak's sky aarti and the Bhagats' answers
Guru Ram Das's song of the wedding horse

games.q: who sang which aarti — tap the pairs.

s: gagan mai thaal sits in Raga Dhanasri
Guru Nanak's sky aarti is in Dhanasri, and the Bhagats' aartis come near the raga's end.
the Bhagats' aartis all describe the sky
Ravidas turns inward to the Name, and Dhanna asks for what a household needs.

games.q: you're Dhanna the farmer, singing to the Lord. what do you put on the tray?
o: the sun, the moon and the stars.
lentils, flour, ghee, shoes, a milk cow.
games.why: Dhanna asks plainly for what a household needs, and the Granth keeps his kitchen-table aarti beside Guru Nanak's sky.

practice: If you'd like, let your attention move outward the way Guru Nanak's hymn does, to the light in the room and whatever sky is above the roof, then inward the way Ravidas does, to one word resting in the breath.
Then set it down the way Dhanna does, on one plain thing your household needs, and let yourself want it honestly; if you pray, Waheguru can mark each step.

wordCard.voice: A hymn in Dhanasri. Guru Nanak's aarti with the sky as the platter, answered near the raga's end by the aartis of Ravidas, Sain and Dhanna. Today's word.

orig.note: aarti, honoring what is dear by waving light before it; Dhanasri holds several.

carryVoice: Your line: the sky's aarti. The platter is already lit. A week of ragas, done.
